newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Digital fears, management changes hit BSkyB.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Digital fears, management changes hit BSkyB.

text.p: BSkyB shares lost 770 million pounds ($1.3 billion) in value on Wednesday on a report the pay television company could be shut out of the bidding for new digital TV licences and the loss of key executives.

The Financial Times said the Independent Television Commission (ITC) had told BSkyB it should drop its equity stake in a consortium with commercial TV groups Carlton and Granada which has applied for digital terrestrial television (DTT) licences.
The report said the consortium - British Digital Broadcasting - could be ruled out of the reckoning on competition grounds if BSkyB did not comply.

An ITC spokeswoman dismissed the report as "speculation". She said the ITC hoped to make a decision by the end of June on whether to award the licences to British Digital Broadcasting or a rival consortium run by cable and broadcast group NTL Inc.
BSkyB confirmed that its deputy managing director David Chance would switch to a consultancy role with the company next year.
The announcement came 24 hours after BSkyB said chief executive Sam Chisholm would give up his job in December on medical grounds.
Chance had been seen as a likely successor to Chisholm but did not apply for the chief executive's job. British media reports said Chance, 40, had also recently been in poor health.
Mark Booth will move from Japan's JSkyB, another part of Rupert Murdoch's global television empire, to replace the highly regarded Chisholm.
BSkyB shares closed 45p lower at 521.5p -- almost eight percent -- on the Financial Times report and management upheaval.
Share analysts said the threatened ITC move could loosen BSkyB's grip on British households and thwart its terrestrial ambitions.
Granada, which owns a 10.8 percent stake in BSkyB, slipped 8.5p to 852.5p but Carlton went the other way, gaining 10.5p to 520.5p.
"The report seems to suggest that the ITC wants to give the licences to British Digital Broadcasting but wants it to fine tune its application," said one analyst.
"Carlton may end up more in the driving seat."

The report said the consortium's shareholders, who have pledged to pump 300 million pounds into the venture, were discussing how to respond to the ITC. It said that BSkyB may withdraw as an equity investor while negotiating a deal to supply sports and movie channels.

The move into digital broadcasting is the next step in the development of BSkyB, which has grown into one of Britain's most successful companies under the leadership of combative New Zealander Chisholm.

The company plans to launch 200-channel digital satellite services into Britain next year and has joined forces with partners including British Telecommunications to offer services such as home shopping.
DTT, a technology which Britain is helping to pioneer, offers a more modest 30 or so channels and less scope for interactive services.

But its advantage is that it is broadcast from land-based transmitters to ordinary aerials. Viewers will need to buy a set-top box or decoder, expected to retail at between 200-300 pounds, to receive the signals but will not require a satellite dish or cable connection. DTT's advocates believe it will prove popular with many of the 75 percent of British households that have not signed up to multi-channel cable or satellite services over the past decade.
Existing "free-to-air" broadcasters such as the BBC and ITV commercial network have been reserved space on DTT to broadcast existing and new services.

Three other blocks of frequencies, capable of carrying 15 channels or more, are being contested by the British Digital Broadcasting consortium and its rival Digital Television Network. ($ = 0.610 British Pounds)
